summary: This Informational document records experiments in configuring UDP socket APIs for ECN, done to get ECN working on UDP for Chromium on Apple, Linux, and Windows platforms. It is a snapshot of the situation.

plainLanguage.summary: Notes on how to tell a program how to watch for "slow down" signals on three kinds of computers.

questions: how to enable ecn on udp socket
ecn socket api linux windows macos
subtitle: How to configure UDP sockets to use explicit congestion notification on Linux, Apple, and Windows.

tldr.problem: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) signals network congestion to endpoints, but UDP socket APIs for receiving and sending ECN codepoints are poorly documented across operating systems.
tldr.mechanism: This document records how to enable ECN on UDP sockets across Linux, Apple, and Windows platforms using socket options and ancillary data in system calls.
tldr.outcome: Applications like QUIC can now use ECN over UDP consistently across platforms to improve congestion control responsiveness.

facts.label: Platforms covered
facts.value: Linux, Apple (macOS and iOS), Windows, FreeBSD

today: RFC 10055 is Informational and documents the state of ECN on UDP socket APIs as of October 2026. It is not a standards-track document and does not mandate any platform behavior, but captures experience from Chromium's efforts to implement QUIC with ECN support.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) is a 2-bit field in the IP header that provides network feedback about congestion. Historically this mattered most for TCP, where the kernel handles ECN internally. However, QUIC, which runs over UDP, has become widely deployed and created a need for ECN support in UDP socket APIs.

This document records the results of getting ECN working over UDP for Chromium on Apple, Linux, and Windows, addressing the fact that platform documentation for these APIs is sparse. It is informational and captures the state as of the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks have a way to tell programs "I'm getting busy, slow down." For a long time, only the fanciest programs (TCP) knew how to listen. Now a faster protocol called QUIC needs to hear these messages too, and different computers have different ways of letting programs listen.

sections.title: Configuring Sockets for ECN
sections.content:
To receive ECN feedback, a program must first enable ECN reporting on the socket, then retrieve the codepoint from each arriving packet. Sending ECN codepoints can be configured either once per socket or individually per packet.

Receiving ECN codepoints: On Linux, Apple, and FreeBSD, IPv4 sockets use the socket option IP_RECVTOS and IPv6 sockets use IPV6_RECVTCLASS. On Linux, dual-stack IPv6 sockets also need IP_RECVTOS to receive ECN for IPv4 packets, but this is not necessary on Apple or FreeBSD. On Windows, the recommended function is WSASetRecvIPEcn() (available since Windows 10 Build 20348), though setsockopt() with IP_RECVECN or IPV6_RECVECN also works. All platforms require the recvmsg() system call to retrieve ECN data as ancillary data (cmsg structures). On Linux and Apple, the two least significant bits of the retrieved byte contain the ECN codepoint, while Windows provides the ECN codepoint directly.

Sending ECN codepoints per socket: On Apple, FreeBSD, and Linux, use the socket options IP_TOS (for IPv4) or IPV6_TCLASS (for IPv6). On Windows, there is no per-socket API for sending ECN codepoints; servers that receive all packets on a single socket must use per-packet marking instead. On non-Apple platforms, setting the ToS byte also sets the DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point), so applications should preserve existing DSCP values.

Sending ECN codepoints per packet: Use ancillary data with sendmsg(). On all three platforms, the cmsg level and type differ slightly. On Linux and Apple, both use IP_TOS or IPV6_TCLASS; FreeBSD uses unsigned char instead of int for IPv4. On Windows, IPv4 packets use IP_ECN and IPv6 use IPV6_ECN.
sections.plainLanguage: To listen for congestion signals, you first tell the computer's network layer to watch for them, then you use a special system call that hands you the message along with the data. To send congestion signals, you can either set it once for all messages from that connection, or mark each message separately. Different computers have different ways to do this.

sections.title: Platform Differences and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The three platforms differ significantly in their ECN socket APIs. Linux and Apple are largely similar, using the same socket option names for both receiving and sending ECN. Windows has a dedicated receiving function (WSASetRecvIPEcn()) and requires per-packet sending via sendmsg(). FreeBSD is close to Linux and Apple but requires unsigned char for IPv4 per-packet sends instead of int.

One notable difference: on Apple platforms, a higher-level network framework alternative exists (NWProtocolIP.Metadata) that provides ECN handling without traditional socket option semantics, though this document focuses on the standard socket APIs.

Applications targeting multiple platforms must handle these variations, such as adapting to Windows' lack of per-socket sending and detecting IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses that behave differently on Windows. Using the ecn-examples code repository can verify implementations across platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: Apple and Linux computers talk about network signals in nearly the same way, but Windows has its own style. All three handle some edge cases (like when IPv6 addresses pretend to be IPv4) differently, so your program needs to know which computer it's running on.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Implementing ECN support on different platforms can help peers identify the operating system in use by a host, which has privacy implications. This document aims to mitigate that possibility by documenting the APIs across platforms, reducing the likelihood that differing ECN capabilities will reveal what operating system is in use.

The ECN field itself is part of the standard IP header and is not encrypted, so network observers can see ECN codepoints in transit. ECN-aware middleboxes (routers and switches) may legitimately modify ECN codepoints to signal congestion, as defined in RFC 3168.

Applications using ECN should be aware that the ECN codepoints are mutable in transit and that this feedback mechanism requires trust that the network operator and equipment are following the ECN specification correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers using ECN differently might give away what they are. Also, ECN fields are not secret, so routers along the way can see and change them. That is by design—it is how the network tells you it is getting busy.
